article.title: Electoral College’s Days May Be Numbered
article.author: Karen Dolan
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Democracy can be messy, but one thing should be simple: If you win the most votes, you should win the election. Unfortunately, when it comes to the highest office in the United States, that’s not always the case. But after the latest election results, we may be closer than ever to fixing this egregious flaw in our democracy. To elect presidents, we rely on the Electoral College . Rather than a national popular vote, the Electoral College decides the presidential election by counting “electoral votes” allocated to states. This undemocratic process resulted from compromises with slave-holding states seeking more political power. In 1787, when delegates convened in Philadelphia to draft the Constitution , one of the most contentious issues was how to choose the president. Some wanted a national popular vote, while others argued that the new country was too large — and without sufficient communication — for voters to get adequate information about the presidential candidates. The Electoral College emerged as a compromise: each state received electoral votes based on its congressional delegation. Related: We All Pay the Price When We Divest in People This had the effect of giving more power to slave-holding states. Because the Constitution’s Three-Fifths Compromise counted three-fifths of their enslaved populations toward congressional representation (even as enslaved people were denied civil, political, and human rights), it gave slave-holding states outsized power in presidential elections. Today, the rationale no longer exists. Slavery was abolished. And with modern telecommunications, Americans from all across the country have ample information available about presidential candidates. Yet the system persists. As a result, the vast majority of Americans who live in solidly “red” or “blue” states, regardless of their size, get ignored during presidential campaigns because one candidate or another can count on winning their electoral votes. Instead, elections revolve entirely around a few “swing states.” This system also means a president can win a majority of electoral votes while losing the national popular vote — which has had significant consequences historically. In 1876, Rutherford B. Hayes won the presidency despite losing the national popular vote to Samuel Tilden. A congressional commission awarded the election to Hayes — aided by the Compromise of 1877 , in which Hayes agreed to remove federal troops from the South, where they had been since the Civil War. This effectively ended Reconstruction and ushered in the age of Jim Crow . In 2000, George W. Bush won Florida’s electoral votes, and the 2000 election, after the Supreme Court stopped a recount. Yet Bush had lost the popular vote by over half a million. In 2016, Donald Trump won the Electoral College despite losing the popular vote to Hillary Clinton by nearly 3 million. It’s no wonder a vast majority of Americans favor abolishing the Electoral College. But how? The Electoral College can only be formally abolished with a constitutional amendment, which is unlikely anytime soon. But the Constitution leaves states to decide how to allocate their electoral votes — and that creates an opening to reform the system. Related: Government Shutdown Causing Healthcare Crisis Today’s National Popular Vote Interstate Compact , an agreement that states can opt into, builds on this provision. Participating states pledge their Electoral College votes to whoever wins the national popular vote — as opposed to the vote in their state alone. Currently, the compact has 18 state signatories and the District of Columbia, totaling 222 Electoral College votes. The compact takes effect when the Electoral College votes reach 270 — the number needed to win the presidency. After the latest elections, Democrats will have new trifectas in Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin. Of these states, Minnesota is already a signatory. If the others join, they’ll have enough votes to meet the threshold . And since these are swing states, that would essentially guarantee the Electoral College winner must also win the national popular vote — the way democracy is supposed to work. It’s past time to make every vote count. Anyone invested in democracy should urge their state to join the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, so all our votes count equally. The possibility is ripe — the time is now. OtherWords
